chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) judged that there would be no burden upon the blood relatives (diyah payers) except for the bone-exposing injury upwards.
And he (peace be upon him) said: What is below the reaching-of-bone injury, the fee of the doctor is in addition to the wergild.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or wergild paid to the victim or their heirs for bodily injury or death.
key_terms.السِّمْحَاق: A specific level of injury, often interpreted as reaching the bone but not fully exposing it, or a minor bone injury.
key_terms.الْعَاقِلَة: The group of male relatives responsible for paying blood money (diyah) on behalf of the offender.
key_terms.الْمُوضِحَة: An injury that exposes the bone.

ai.seo_question: Who pays for medical fees in minor injuries according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the precedent set by Amir al-Mu'minin (AS) regarding the division of liability in bodily injuries, distinguishing between deep wounds where the bone is exposed (falling on the 'Aqilah) and superficial flesh wounds (where medical fees are separate from the blood money). This ruling highlights the jurisprudential precision in allocating financial responsibility based on the severity and depth of the injury, ensuring that the 'Aqilah bears the cost of significant structural damage while minor injuries are handled differently.
